claims.quote: Other wrappers sharing that alias can borrow from this pool, even though the callback’s timezone, settings, and operations belong to the first wrapper.

known_problems.reason: The item faults that "the process-wide pool registry is keyed only by database alias", which is the cause the answer key gives for GT-v2 (one pool cached per alias with the parameters of its first use). Its own reason is the callback's time zone, settings and operations, a different matter; it never says a test run uses the earlier database or that a clone is blocked.

claims.notes: Situation: two DatabaseWrapper objects for one alias with pooling on. The item says the pool registry is keyed only by alias and keeps the first wrapper's bound `_configure_connection`, so a second wrapper borrows from a pool configured through the first wrapper. True: a run at head built one pool for two wrappers of the alias, its configure callback was bound to the first wrapper, and a wrapper whose NAME was then changed still got the pool for the first NAME. The keying objection is the cause of GT-v2, but the item states none of GT-v2's results. What it says beyond that cause is the callback mismatch. The change adds this code, so it is responsible. Nothing documents or tests wrappers of one alias with differing time zone, settings or operations, the item names no use that fails (it calls the time-zone case a workaround already in place: ensure_timezone() closes the pool), and nothing is shown to stop working, so it is a design improvement. GT-v6 was checked: the item calls the registry process-wide but objects to its key, not to a pool surviving a fork, so no entry. GT-v1, GT-v5 and GT-v11 were checked: their cause is what the callback calls (compose_sql on the wrapper, module functions instead of methods), which the item does not fault.
evidence: clone/django/db/backends/postgresql/base.py:200-241: `_connection_pools = {}` is a class attribute, looked up by self.alias only; the pool is built with configure=self._configure_connection.
clone/django/db/backends/postgresql/base.py:369-383: _configure_connection reads self.ops, self.timezone_name and self.settings_dict of the wrapper it is bound to.

Run clone-work/check_pool.py at head (psycopg 3.3.6, psycopg_pool 3.3.3, no server needed): two copies of the default wrapper returned the same pool object, one pool constructed, callback bound to first wrapper True and to second False; after changing the second wrapper's NAME its pool was still the first one with dbname db_a.
clone/django/db/backends/postgresql/base.py:362-367 and clone/django/test/signals.py:82: ensure_timezone() closes the pool on a time zone change.

1.note: Two statements joined by "Separately": one about cleanup building a pool, one about the private `_pool` attribute. Either can be true without the other, so they are two claims.

claims.quote: cleanup paths such as `ensure_timezone()` and database teardown can initialize a pool merely to close it
claims.notes: Situation: close_pool() is called on a wrapper with the pool option set and no pool yet for its alias. The item says the `pool` property both builds and returns the pool, so cleanup builds one only to close it. True: close_pool() tests `self.pool`, which constructs and registers a ConnectionPool when none exists. A run at head with an empty registry showed close_pool() and ensure_timezone() each construct one pool and leave the registry empty again. The change adds this code, so it is responsible. Nothing stops working: the pool is built with open=False, never opened, and removed at once, and the item names no failure, so no promise is in play and it is an improvement. Checked against every known problem: GT-v2's cause is a pool kept per alias with its first parameters and reused by the _nodb_cursor fallback, not cleanup constructing a pool, and the item states none of GT-v2's results; no entry.
evidence: clone/django/db/backends/postgresql/base.py:202-246: the pool property constructs and caches; close_pool() is `if self.pool: self.pool.close(); del self._connection_pools[self.alias]`.
clone/django/db/backends/postgresql/base.py:362-364, clone/django/db/backends/postgresql/creation.py:61 and 90, clone/django/test/signals.py:82: the cleanup callers of close_pool().

Run clone-work/check_pool.py at head (psycopg 3.3.6, psycopg_pool 3.3.3, no server needed): registry before {}, pools constructed by close_pool(): 1, registry after {}, pools constructed by ensure_timezone(): 1.

claims.quote: retrieves the owning pool through `connection._pool`, coupling Django to a private psycopg implementation detail
claims.notes: Situation: a pooled connection is returned in _close(). The item says Django finds the pool through the connection's private `_pool` attribute. True: base.py:395 calls self.connection._pool.putconn(self.connection), and in the installed psycopg `_pool` is an underscore attribute of the connection with no public `pool` counterpart. The change adds the line, so it is responsible. It works with the pool versions the change pins; the concern is a later psycopg release changing a private name, which nothing promises, so it is an improvement. It bears on no known problem: none has `_pool` access as its cause or result.
evidence: clone/django/db/backends/postgresql/base.py:391-397: `self.connection._pool.putconn(self.connection)`, with a comment calling it a workaround for tests.
Run clone-work/check_pool.py: psycopg._connection_base declares `self._pool: BasePool | None`; psycopg.Connection has no public `pool` attribute.
